paragraphs: AdaNovo addresses a problem in identifying peptides from tandem mass spectra: the training examples can systematically favor some amino acids and provide unreliable evidence for others. Modified amino acids appear less frequently than ordinary ones, making them harder for existing models to identify. Noise and missing peaks also weaken the reliability of the associations between spectra and peptide sequences.

The proposed framework uses conditional mutual information between a spectrum and an amino acid or peptide to guide robust training. This information-based quantity concerns how much one variable tells us about another after accounting for conditioning information. AdaNovo brings that perspective into peptide sequencing, using domain knowledge to address both underrepresented modifications and unreliable training matches.

Experiments report better performance than previous competitors on the nine-species benchmark, alongside improvements of 3.6%–9.4% in identifying post-translational modifications. These findings connect improved sequencing with better handling of a biologically meaningful source of training imbalance. They support the framework’s effectiveness on the reported evaluations without implying that all kinds of mass-spectrum noise or data bias have been eliminated.
neurips-2024-adanovo-towards-robust-emph.tldr: AdaNovo uses conditional mutual information to improve peptide sequencing under training biases involving rare modifications and unreliable spectra.

paragraphs: Cross-modal retrieval searches across different kinds of content, such as finding images that match text. Hashing makes this practical by representing content with compact codes that support inexpensive storage and fast search. The paper identifies a weakness in existing approaches: their representations and semantic associations can miss information needed to connect images and text effectively.

EGATH combines several components in an end-to-end system. CLIP and a Transformer help represent semantic consistency across modalities. A classifier built with a graph attention network supplies predicted labels that further strengthen the features used for retrieval. The system then constructs hash codes through an optimization strategy and loss function designed to retain semantic information while keeping the codes compact.

Experiments on NUS-WIDE, MIRFlickr25K, and MS-COCO report significant improvements over several state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is therefore a coordinated approach to representation and compression: richer image–text associations inform the compact codes used for search. The reported results support that combination on the evaluated retrieval benchmarks.
neurips-2024-an-end-to-end-graph-attenti.tldr: EGATH combines image–text representations and graph attention to create compact hash codes with improved cross-modal retrieval performance.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether combining predictors should work differently when prediction follows the direction from cause to effect versus the reverse direction. It studies a simple setting with one binary target and two continuous predictors. Keeping the data the same makes it possible to examine how assumptions about causal direction change the merged predictor.

The merging rule uses Causal Maximum Entropy, or CMAXENT, as its inductive bias: the principle that guides the choice among solutions compatible with the available information. When every pairwise distribution is observed, the authors show that this rule produces logistic regression in the causal direction and Linear Discriminant Analysis in the anticausal direction. Thus, the directional assumption leads to distinct familiar prediction rules.

The analysis also considers cases where only some pairwise distributions are available, examining differences in the resulting decision boundaries and their implications for Out-Of-Variable generalization. The authors expect related asymmetries in other merging methods that account for cause–effect differences, but that broader expectation is separate from the specific CMAXENT results.
neurips-2024-causal-vs-anticausal-mergin.tldr: Under CMAXENT, merging predictors from the same data yields different solutions depending on whether prediction follows or reverses causal direction.

paragraphs: Semantic scene completion reconstructs a three-dimensional scene and assigns semantic meaning to its contents from visual inputs. The paper highlights two problems in existing approaches. Queries shared across images may gather features without adapting to each scene’s relevant regions. Meanwhile, different 3D points can project to the same image location, creating ambiguity when depth is not represented.

CGFormer addresses these problems with a context and geometry aware voxel transformer. Its query generator adapts queries to the individual image, helping direct information gathering toward relevant regions. Its deformable cross-attention operates in 3D pixel space, using depth coordinates to distinguish points with similar image coordinates. The network also combines voxel and TPV representations to strengthen local and global semantic and geometric information.

The reported results reach state-of-the-art performance on SemanticKITTI and SSCBench-KITTI-360, with mIoU scores of 16.87 and 20.05, respectively. CGFormer also outperforms evaluated approaches that use temporal images or substantially larger image backbones. These findings support the value of adapting feature collection to both scene content and depth.
neurips-2024-context-and-geometry-aware-.tldr: CGFormer improves semantic scene completion by adapting attention to each image’s content and distinguishing projected points through depth.

paragraphs: D-LLM starts from the idea that different tokens do not always need the same amount of computation. Processing every token equivalently can spend resources on words that contribute little to a particular question. The paper proposes dynamic inference that adjusts resource allocation during token processing, targeting the computational demands that make large language models difficult to deploy on constrained platforms.

Each Transformer layer receives a decision module that chooses whether a network unit should run or be skipped. Skipping creates a practical complication: the corresponding key and value information may be absent from the KV cache used by later attention calculations. D-LLM introduces an eviction policy that excludes skipped layers from subsequent attention, addressing this incompatibility while reducing storage requirements.

Experiments report reductions of up to 45% in computational cost and KV storage for question answering, summarization, and mathematical problem solving, and up to 50% for commonsense reasoning. These are reported upper reductions across the evaluated tasks. The contribution combines adaptive execution with a cache policy that makes skipping usable in inference applications.
neurips-2024-d-llm-a-token-adaptive-comp.tldr: D-LLM dynamically skips computation for tokens and manages the resulting missing cache entries to reduce inference compute and storage.

paragraphs: DiffusionPID investigates how words in a text prompt influence images produced by diffusion models. A prompt contains individual concepts, but its effect also depends on relationships among words. The paper introduces an information-theoretic approach for examining those contributions, addressing questions about how these models represent visual meaning and why their behavior can be difficult to interpret.

The method applies partial information decomposition to the denoising model at both image and pixel levels. It separates unique information associated with individual tokens, redundant information shared across tokens, and synergistic information arising from their interactions. This provides a framework for asking both where a concept is expressed and how combinations of words shape the output.

The authors use the method to analyze concept localization, recover gender and ethnicity biases, and visualize word ambiguity and similarity from the model’s perspective. They also demonstrate its usefulness for prompt intervention. These applications position DiffusionPID as a diagnostic tool: its contribution is an account of token effects and interactions that can support closer examination of generated images.
neurips-2024-diffusion-pid-interpreting-.tldr: DiffusionPID separates individual and interacting token contributions to diagnose how text prompts shape diffusion-generated images.

paragraphs: Dataset valuation asks how much adding one dataset helps a machine learning task when other datasets are already available. The answer depends on a predefined measure of utility, so the object being valued is the dataset’s incremental contribution to that measure. The Shapley value offers a principled way to assign such contributions, backed by formal axioms.

Computing Shapley values can be expensive, and generic Monte Carlo approximations can remain costly. DU-Shapley uses structure specific to dataset valuation to construct a more efficient approximation. Its discrete uniform formulation expresses the approximation as an expectation over a distribution with a manageable number of possible values, giving the estimation problem a more tractable form.

The paper supports this approach with both asymptotic and non-asymptotic theoretical guarantees, addressing behavior at large scales as well as finite settings. Numerical experiments illustrate its benefits. The result is a proxy intended to make principled dataset valuation more practical, with its efficiency coming from problem structure rather than relying only on a generic sampling approximation.
neurips-2024-du-shapley-a-shapley-value-.tldr: DU-Shapley uses dataset-valuation structure to approximate Shapley values more efficiently, supported by theory and numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Adversarial training improves robustness by exposing a model to attacks during training, but finding attacks made of discrete text tokens is computationally expensive. This paper instead computes attacks in the model’s continuous embedding space. The authors report that generating these perturbations is orders of magnitude more efficient, making repeated adversarial training steps more practical.

The paper introduces two algorithms. C-AdvUL combines a loss for resisting continuous attacks on an adversarial behavior dataset with a separate fine-tuning loss on utility data. The second component preserves useful behavior alongside robustness. C-AdvIPO provides an adversarial variant of IPO that does not require utility data, offering another route to robust alignment.

Evaluations cover five models from several families and scales, testing robustness against the discrete attacks GCG, AutoDAN, and PAIR. Both algorithms substantially improve resistance while maintaining utility in those experiments. The central finding is empirical transfer: training against continuous perturbations can improve robustness to discrete attacks. It supports a more scalable training approach without establishing protection against every possible textual attack.
neurips-2024-efficient-adversarial-train.tldr: Training against efficient continuous embedding attacks improves resistance to tested discrete language-model attacks while maintaining utility.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search can only discover networks that its search space permits. The paper argues that many existing spaces are too restricted to enable substantial changes in network design. If the available building blocks already impose a narrow architectural pattern, even effective search may produce variations of that pattern rather than substantially different structures.

Einspace expands the available designs through a parameterized probabilistic context-free grammar. This grammar builds architectures from fundamental operations and can represent networks of different sizes and complexity, including convolution and attention components. It encompasses existing competitive architectures while leaving room for new combinations. The search-space design is therefore a central contribution, alongside the architectures discovered within it.

Experiments on the diverse Unseen NAS datasets find competitive networks when searching from scratch. Starting from strong baseline architectures consistently produces large improvements in the reported experiments. These findings support both broader expressivity and strategic initialization as useful ingredients for architecture search. They advance the possibility of more substantial automated design changes without claiming that such a transformation has already been achieved.
neurips-2024-einspace-searching-for-neur.tldr: Einspace uses a grammar of fundamental operations to broaden neural architecture search and improve architectures, especially from strong starting points.

paragraphs: Vision-language models such as CLIP depend on the text descriptions used to recognize image categories. Optimizing these prompts with labeled examples can help, but requires annotation work. The paper also identifies label bias inherited from imbalanced pretraining data as a separate source of reduced performance. Frolic addresses both issues without requiring labeled downstream data.

The framework learns distributions over prompt prototypes to capture diverse visual representations. It combines these with the original CLIP model through confidence matching, then applies a label-free adjustment to the output logits to correct label bias. The approach is described as training-free and avoids hyperparameter tuning, so the proposed adaptation does not rely on a conventional labeled prompt-training procedure.

Experiments span 16 datasets. With CLIP ViT-B/16, Frolic reports an average improvement of 2.6% over the state of the art on ten datasets and an average margin of 1.5% on ImageNet and five distribution shifts. These results support combining prompt diversity with bias correction as a practical way to improve the evaluated zero-shot predictions.
neurips-2024-enhancing-zero-shot-vision-.tldr: Frolic improves zero-shot CLIP predictions through prompt distributions, confidence-based fusion, and label-bias correction without labeled data or training.

paragraphs: Reward models help guide language models toward responses that match human preferences, making the quality of their training data consequential. HelpSteer2 addresses the need for updated preference data as language models improve. It also offers a permissive CC-BY-4.0 license, addressing usage restrictions associated with some preference datasets distilled from proprietary models.

The dataset contains ten thousand response pairs and emphasizes improvements in both generated responses and attribute labeling. A reward model based on Nemotron-4-340B and trained with HelpSteer2 achieves 92.0% on Reward-Bench’s primary dataset. The paper reports that this exceeded the listed open and proprietary models as of June 12, 2024. That result belongs to the particular model-and-dataset combination and the stated comparison date.

Despite being an order of magnitude smaller than datasets such as HH-RLHF, HelpSteer2 supports effective reward-model training in the reported experiments. The authors also show that its reward models help align language models and introduce SteerLM 2.0 to use their multiple attribute scores. Together, the contributions connect compact preference data with practical alignment methods.
neurips-2024-helpsteer-2-open-source-dat.tldr: HelpSteer2 provides ten thousand permissively licensed response pairs that support strong reward modeling and multi-attribute language-model alignment.

paragraphs: JiuZhang3.0 tackles the expense of obtaining large amounts of mathematical training material. Existing approaches can require extensive pretraining text or large-scale problem generation by a stronger language model. This paper trains a smaller language model to synthesize mathematical problems, using a limited amount of GPT-4-generated supervision to transfer the data-generation capability.

The supervision combines prompts organized around human educational stages with selected mathematical texts. The prompts encourage coverage of varied knowledge and difficulty levels, while gradient-based influence estimation identifies valuable source texts. GPT-4 uses these inputs to create a distillation dataset for the smaller synthesis model. That model then generates six million problems for pretraining JiuZhang3.0.

The reported process uses 9.3 thousand GPT-4 API calls and 4.6B of training data. JiuZhang3.0 achieves state-of-the-art results on several mathematical reasoning datasets in both natural-language reasoning and tool-manipulation settings. The findings support concentrating stronger-model assistance on training a reusable data generator, allowing the smaller model to carry out the subsequent large-scale synthesis.
neurips-2024-jiuzhang3-0-efficiently-imp.tldr: JiuZhang3.0 transfers mathematical problem synthesis from GPT-4 to a smaller model to generate large-scale training data efficiently.

paragraphs: Image inverse problems recover an image from incomplete or degraded observations, using prior knowledge about plausible images to guide reconstruction. Diffusion models can learn this knowledge, but training on whole images demands substantial data and computation. Those costs become especially restrictive for high-resolution and high-dimensional images, motivating a way to learn from smaller image pieces.

PaDIS trains a position-aware diffusion model on patches. It combines patch scores with positional encodings to obtain a score function for the entire image, then uses that function as the reconstruction prior. Position information allows the approach to retain whole-image generation capability despite patch-based training. The resulting prior can also be used with different diffusion inverse solvers.

The authors demonstrate improved memory and data efficiency and apply the method to CT reconstruction, deblurring, and superresolution in natural and medical imaging. Under limited training data, PaDIS outperforms earlier diffusion inverse solvers trained with whole-image priors. That qualification matters: the reported advantage specifically supports patch-based learning as an effective strategy when training data are scarce.
neurips-2024-learning-image-priors-throu.tldr: PaDIS builds whole-image diffusion priors from position-aware patches, improving reconstruction efficiency and performance when training data are limited.

paragraphs: Many machine learning problems involve several objectives at once, such as performance across multiple tasks or goals involving fairness and robustness. Multiobjective optimization studies these objectives jointly through Pareto optimality and Pareto set learning. Its aim is to represent meaningful tradeoffs among objectives, rather than express the entire problem through one combined scalar objective.

The paper identifies a mismatch between this need and existing benchmark libraries. Those libraries mainly emphasize evolutionary algorithms, including methods that use objective evaluations without effectively exploiting derivative information. The authors argue that these approaches do not scale effectively to models with millions of parameters, creating a gap for tools suited to large machine learning systems.

LibMOON is a PyTorch library designed around gradient-based multiobjective optimization methods. It brings together state-of-the-art methods and provides an open-source framework for fair, comprehensive benchmarking. The contribution is shared infrastructure for studying and comparing these approaches, making gradient-based optimization more accessible in settings with many parameters and competing goals. The abstract presents that infrastructure rather than a particular numerical performance result.
neurips-2024-libmoon-a-gradient-based-mu.tldr: LibMOON provides an open-source PyTorch library and benchmark framework for gradient-based optimization of multiple competing objectives.

paragraphs: Generating a useful articulated 3D object requires both its geometry and a coherent account of how its parts move. MIDGArD organizes this problem into two connected stages: structure generation and shape generation. The separation gives the system an explicit structural description to work with before it produces the meshes that make up the final asset.

The structure module represents structural and motion-related attributes as graph features. It progressively removes noise from these features to produce coherent, interpretable articulation, including when inputs are noisy or incomplete. The resulting graph then conditions a 3D shape generator, which fills each link of the articulated structure with a consistent mesh. This connects the object’s appearance to its generated movement structure.

Experiments report improvements in asset quality, consistency, and interpretability. The generated objects are also fully simulatable and can integrate with standard physics engines such as MuJoCo. This matters because the output includes the articulation needed for simulation, extending its potential use beyond static content to applications involving interaction, including robotics and digital environments.
neurips-2024-midgard-modular-interpretab.tldr: MIDGArD generates simulatable articulated 3D assets by first denoising a structural graph and then generating meshes conditioned on it.

paragraphs: Personalized talking-face generation aims to preserve both a person’s appearance and their characteristic way of speaking. Previous approaches often train a separate neural radiance field for each identity, storing appearance and motion together. MimicTalk addresses the inefficiency and limited generalization associated with that repeated training process by starting from a generic model shared across people.

The method first builds a person-agnostic 3D talking-face model and then adapts it to a specific identity. A hybrid adaptation process learns static appearance and dynamic facial features. Separately, an in-context audio-to-motion model uses a reference video to mimic the person’s talking style, avoiding the information loss associated with compressing that style into an explicit representation.

The authors report adaptation to an unseen identity in 15 minutes, a 47-fold speedup over previous person-dependent methods. Experiments also show improvements over previous baselines in video quality and expressiveness. The contribution therefore combines reusable generic knowledge with personalized adaptation, addressing the time needed to capture a new identity while retaining attention to how that person looks and moves.
neurips-2024-mimictalk-mimicking-a-perso.tldr: MimicTalk adapts a generic 3D talking-face model to a new person in 15 minutes while capturing appearance and expressive talking style.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust reinforcement learning optimizes performance against the worst environment within a specified uncertainty set around a nominal model. This offers a way to account for differences between training and deployment environments. The paper asks how many samples are needed to solve these robust problems, particularly when uncertainty is measured using generalized Lp norms.

The analysis assumes access to a generative model that can sample from the nominal Markov decision process. It considers two common structures for the uncertainty set, called state-action rectangular and state rectangular. Within these settings, the results imply that robust problems can require fewer samples than standard reinforcement learning problems. This is a possibility established under the analyzed setup, rather than a universal advantage of robustness.

For state-action rectangular uncertainty, the paper gives a near-optimal upper bound and a matching minimax lower bound. For state rectangular uncertainty, it improves the existing upper bound and establishes tightness through a lower bound using the L-infinity norm. These results clarify the statistical cost of robustness and identify settings where established complexity bounds can be sharpened.
neurips-2024-near-optimal-distributional.tldr: The paper sharpens sample-complexity bounds for robust reinforcement learning with generalized Lp uncertainty and shows it can be more sample-efficient than standard RL.

paragraphs: Proving a neural controller safe indefinitely requires reasoning about both the network and the physical system it controls. VerSAILLE connects these tasks through a control envelope already proved safe in differential dynamic logic. From that envelope, it derives a specification for the neural network. Proving that the network satisfies this specification yields a corresponding infinite-time safety proof for the controlled system.

A technical obstacle is that these specifications can contain nonlinear arithmetic and complex logical structure, whereas efficient neural-network verification tools often support only linear constraints. The paper introduces Mosaic to bridge that gap. For polynomial real-arithmetic properties of piecewise-linear networks, Mosaic provides sound and complete verification by splitting queries and combining approximation with exact reasoning about counterexample regions.

On the Vertical Airborne Collision Avoidance benchmark, the approach proves infinite-time safety for some scenarios and exhaustively enumerates counterexample regions in unsafe ones. It also substantially outperforms evaluated closed-loop verification tools. The safety conclusion remains tied to the proved envelope and verified network specification; the method establishes that connection rather than assuming every tested controller is safe.
neurips-2024-provably-safe-neural-networ.tldr: VerSAILLE links neural-network specifications to infinite-time control safety proofs, while Mosaic verifies the nonlinear properties needed for that link.

paragraphs: Many learning algorithms change the data they learn from as training proceeds. Active learning, multi-armed bandits, and self-training all involve a feedback loop: data shape the current model, and the current model influences subsequent training data. This paper names that shared pattern reciprocal learning and formulates it using decision theory.

The common formulation makes it possible to study convergence across these otherwise distinct algorithms. The central mathematical condition is contraction: repeated updates must draw the learning process toward a stable point. When this holds, the Banach fixed-point theorem provides a route to proving convergence. The paper uses this perspective to identify sufficient conditions on both model predictions and data adaptation.

Under assumptions on the loss, probabilistic predictions, and sample adaptation that is non-greedy and either randomized or regularized, the authors establish linear-rate convergence to an approximately optimal model. These conditions are part of the result, not a claim that every reciprocal-learning algorithm converges. Corollaries connect the general theory back to active learning, self-training, and bandits, explaining how their update choices fit the shared framework.
neurips-2024-reciprocal-learning-2660a29.tldr: Reciprocal learning unifies algorithms that jointly update models and training data, establishing convergence under specified contraction-related conditions.

paragraphs: SciInstruct targets gaps in language models’ ability to handle complex scientific concepts, symbolic equations, and advanced numerical calculations. The paper introduces a collection of scientific training instructions intended to support college-level reasoning. Its central challenge is obtaining useful reasoning annotations in scientific domains where suitable training data are scarce.

The annotation framework uses existing language models to generate step-by-step reasoning for scientific questions that lack annotations. It then applies a self-reflective process in which generated reasoning is criticized and revised. The resulting dataset covers physics, chemistry, mathematics, and formal proofs. The authors also analyze its composition across dimensions including subject, scale, source, question type, and answer length.

To evaluate the dataset, the authors fine-tune several models, including two ChatGLM3 sizes, Llama3-8B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B: MetaMath. They report stronger scientific and mathematical reasoning without sacrificing the base models’ language-understanding capabilities. These results support the usefulness of combining generated explanations with critique and revision as a way to create scientific instruction data for multiple language-model families.
neurips-2024-sciinstruct-a-self-reflecti.tldr: SciInstruct uses generated reasoning followed by critique and revision to create scientific training data that improves several language models’ reasoning.

paragraphs: Visual reinforcement learning needs representations that capture how an environment changes. When an agent receives multiple input modalities, those inputs can contain both shared information and meaningful differences. The paper finds that, when modalities are heterogeneous, correlated and distinct features are equally important but play different roles in describing environmental dynamics.

Dissected Dynamics Modeling, or DDM, explicitly separates information that is consistent across modalities from information that is inconsistent. It routes these features through different dynamics-modeling pathways instead of treating their relationships uniformly. This separation introduces implicit regularization during learning. A reward-prediction function further filters out task-irrelevant information from both categories of features, preserving useful distinctions while reducing distractions.

Experiments in challenging multimodal visual environments show consistently competitive performance. The contribution is a way to organize representation learning around the different roles of shared and modality-specific information. Its findings support retaining meaningful differences between inputs while also modeling their common content, with task relevance assessed through reward prediction rather than through cross-modal agreement alone.
neurips-2024-seek-commonality-but-preser.tldr: DDM separates shared and differing multimodal features into dynamics pathways and uses reward prediction to retain task-relevant information.

paragraphs: Models that forecast wildfire spread or backtrack its development need many examples of fire behavior. Sim2Real-Fire explores whether less expensive simulated scenarios can provide training data for analyzing real fires. The central issue is the simulation-to-reality gap: learning useful patterns in a simulator does not by itself establish that those patterns will transfer to real-world wildfire scenarios.

The paper introduces a dataset with one million simulated scenarios and multiple types of environmental information for training. It also prepares one thousand real-world scenarios for testing. This setup gives the study a direct transfer question: how well can models trained using simulated wildfire data perform when evaluated on real fires?

Alongside the dataset, the authors propose S2R-FireTr, a deep Transformer that incorporates the multimodal environmental information for both forecasting and backtracking. It surpasses state-of-the-art methods in the reported real-world evaluation. The result supports the potential of simulation-based training combined with environmental context, while the dataset provides a resource for investigating how to reduce the transfer gap.
neurips-2024-sim2real-fire-a-multi-modal.tldr: Sim2Real-Fire pairs large-scale simulated wildfire training data with real-world testing and a Transformer for forecasting and backtracking fires.

paragraphs: Task-trained recurrent neural networks are used to investigate how neural dynamics might support behavior, but they typically keep recurrent connection weights fixed. Biological synaptic connections can change under the influence of neuromodulators. This paper explores a structured version of that flexibility in low-rank recurrent networks, focusing on the computational effects of dynamically scaling connection strengths.

The proposed NM-RNN contains a neuromodulatory subnetwork that produces a low-dimensional control signal. That signal scales the low-rank recurrent weights of another network responsible for producing outputs. The arrangement allows connectivity to change in a constrained, organized way during computation, giving the model more flexibility while retaining a low-rank structure that the authors can analyze.

In experiments on canonical tasks, NM-RNNs train and generalize more accurately than the compared low-rank RNNs. Theoretical analysis also shows how neuromodulatory gain scaling produces gating mechanisms familiar from artificial recurrent networks. Further analysis of trained dynamics examines how task computations are distributed. Together, these results connect a biologically motivated form of changing connectivity with useful and interpretable computational mechanisms.
neurips-2024-structured-flexibility-in-r.tldr: A neuromodulatory subnetwork dynamically scales recurrent weights, improving tested task performance and providing a theoretical link to gating mechanisms.

paragraphs: Image fusion combines useful information from multiple source images into one result. The paper studies how that combination can adapt at test time while retaining a theoretical justification. It approaches the problem through generalization error, deriving a dynamic fusion paradigm that provably reduces an upper bound on that error within its analysis.

The method decomposes the fused image into components associated with its individual sources. Differences between those components define Relative Dominability, a measure of how strongly a source contributes to constructing the fused image. This quantity highlights dominant regions dynamically and can be converted into fusion weights, allowing contributions to vary with the information supplied by each source.

The theoretical result links reduced generalization error to a negative correlation between the Relative Dominability-based fusion weight and the corresponding single-source reconstruction loss. That relationship is central to the justification; the claim is not that arbitrary dynamic weighting improves generalization. Experiments across multiple benchmarks support the proposed approach and its reported superiority, connecting the theoretical weighting principle with observed fusion performance.
neurips-2024-test-time-dynamic-image-fus.tldr: The paper derives test-time image-fusion weights from source contributions and connects their behavior to a reduced generalization-error bound.

paragraphs: In scenes containing many objects, a vision-language model may focus on something different from the user. Voila-A uses gaze as a proxy for human attention, giving the model an additional signal about what matters in the scene. The paper considers gaze collected through wearable devices, including mixed-reality glasses, as a practical source of this guidance.

The authors collect hundreds of minutes of gaze data and show that localized narratives can mimic human gaze modalities. They then build an automatic annotation pipeline using GPT-4 to create VOILA-COCO. Their VOILA-A model incorporates gaze information while retaining knowledge acquired through large-scale web pretraining, connecting attention guidance with an existing vision-language foundation.

Evaluation uses a held-out validation set and VOILA-GAZE, a newly collected test set of real-life scenarios captured with a gaze-tracking device. Voila-A significantly outperforms several baselines in these experiments. The findings support gaze as useful context for aligning model focus with users, making attention-sensitive interaction a concrete modeling and data-construction problem.
neurips-2024-voila-a-aligning-vision-lan.tldr: Voila-A incorporates gaze into vision-language models to better align their focus with users and improves performance on the reported evaluations.
